title: The Quit-Proof Blueprint
summary: A simple plan to get your key person's knowledge out of their head and into a checklist, then automate the repeat parts. Built for small shops with no spare time.

sections.heading: 1. Find what lives in one head
points: List every task only one person does. Start with invoices, follow-ups, reporting and supplier orders.
Ask: if this person vanished today, what would break first?
Write down every login and tool they use. Note who actually owns each account.
Flag the odd rules, like 'this client always pays late' or 'never email this supplier on Fridays'.
Rank the list by pain. Fix the top three first, not all twenty.

sections.heading: 2. Capture it in one week
points: Ask them to record their screen while doing each task once, talking out loud. Most laptops and phones have a built-in screen recorder, or use a free tool like Loom.
Keep each recording to one task. Short beats thorough.
Turn each recording into a checklist: numbered steps, plain words, one action per line.
Have someone else follow the checklist cold. Wherever they get stuck, the checklist is missing a step.
Store everything in one shared folder that more than one person can open.

sections.heading: 3. Decide what to automate
points: Good candidates: repeatable, rule-based, same steps every time. Examples: creating an invoice from a form, sending a payment reminder, copying order details into a sheet.
Keep human: pricing exceptions, upset clients, anything needing judgment or tact.
Test each step with one question: could I explain this to a stranger using only if/then rules? If yes, automate it.
Start with one task. A small win you trust beats a big build you don't.

sections.heading: 4. Build your first Make.com scenario
points: Pick a trigger: a new form response, a new row in Google Sheets, or a new email.
Add the action: create the document, send the message, or update the row.
Run it with test data before touching anything real.
Turn on error notifications so a failure pings you instead of silently breaking.
Write one line in the checklist: 'This step is now done by the scenario. If it fails, do it by hand like this.'

sections.heading: 5. What to watch for
points: Shared access: put logins in a password manager such as Bitwarden or 1Password, not in one person's head or a sticky note.
Do this while your employee is happy and still here, not in the last week of a notice period.
Position it as backup for the whole team, not a plan to replace anyone.
Review the checklists every few months. Processes drift.
Notice periods and contracts vary, so check yours so you know how much time you would actually have.

title: The Cashless Shop Checklist
summary: A practical checklist to make paying at your shop faster, offer split payments safely, and log every sale without typing. Based on one mall visit, so treat it as ideas to test.

sections.heading: What I saw, and what I can't claim
points: Zara was packed. LC Waikiki, H&M and Max were nearly empty. That is one visit, not data.
Payments were cashless: QR codes, phones and a palm scan.
The app name I kept hearing was Kaspi. Look up how it describes itself.
My guess is that fast, easy paying makes big prices feel smaller. It is a guess, not a finding.
Skip country rankings. 'Developed' means different things on different lists.

sections.heading: Step 1: Make paying take two seconds
points: Time your own checkout from 'ready to pay' to 'receipt'. Write the number down.
Ask five regular customers how they prefer to pay.
Add the methods they already use: card tap, phone wallet, local QR payments.
Use a provider that works in your country, such as Stripe or Square where available.
Remove any step that is not needed, like retyping amounts or asking for paper details.
Watch the fees per method before you switch anything on.

sections.heading: Step 2: Look at split payments carefully
points: Check if your payment provider offers instalments or buy now pay later for your country.
Read who pays the fee, you or the customer, and what happens on refunds.
Check who carries the risk if the customer stops paying.
Only offer it on bigger items where it makes sense.
Be clear about the total price. Do not push anyone into debt.
This is education, not financial advice. Ask an accountant if unsure.

sections.heading: Step 3: Automate the sales log with Make.com
points: Trigger: a new successful payment from your provider (a Stripe module, or a webhook).
Action 1: add a row to Google Sheets with date, item, amount, fee and method.
Action 2: send a Slack or email message for orders above an amount you choose.
Action 3: a daily scenario that sums yesterday's sales and sends you one message.
Test with a small real payment first.
Watch for duplicate rows, refunds and failed payments. Add error handling so you get alerted.

sections.heading: Step 4: Run a two week test
points: Track checkout time, share of cash versus digital, and total fees.
Change one thing at a time so you know what worked.
Ask staff where customers get stuck.
Keep what saves time. Drop what only adds fees.

title: The Invoice Chaser Blueprint
summary: The three message templates, the timing, and the Make.com steps to send them automatically without chasing anyone who has already paid.

sections.heading: The 3-message sequence
points: Message 1, 1 day after the due date: the nudge. Friendly, short, assumes the invoice got buried.
Message 2, 7 days after: the specific ask. Request a payment date and invite any problem with the invoice.
Message 3, 14 days after: the firm close. State what you need, by when, and what happens next under your terms.
Change the tone at each step, not the facts. Same invoice number, amount and link every time.
Adjust the days to fit your payment terms. Treat 1, 7 and 14 as a starting point.

sections.heading: Message templates to copy
points: Message 1: Hi [Name], quick check on invoice [#] for [amount], due [date]. Here is the link in case it got buried: [link]. Shout if you need anything from me.
Message 2: Hi [Name], invoice [#] is now a week overdue. Can you confirm the payment date by [day]? If something looks wrong on the invoice, tell me and I will fix it today.
Message 3: Hi [Name], invoice [#] for [amount] is 14 days overdue. I need payment or a confirmed date by [day]. Call me if that is easier.
Add a consequence line to message 3 only if your contract supports it, for example pausing work on the project.
Keep every message under 60 words and include the link every time.

sections.heading: The Make.com build
points: Keep your invoices in one place, such as a Google Sheet with columns: client, email, invoice number, amount, due date, status, last message sent.
Trigger: a scheduled scenario that runs once a day, at a time that suits your clients.
Work out days overdue: today minus due date. Skip rows marked paid.
Add a Router with three routes and filters for 1, 7 and 14 days overdue. Each route sends its own template.
Send with the Gmail module, or your email tool, filling in name, invoice number, amount and link.
Write back to the sheet: which message was sent and when. This stops duplicates if the scenario runs twice.

sections.heading: Safety checks before it sends
points: Re-read the invoice status right before each send, not just at the start of the run. Someone may have paid in the meantime.
Add a pause column. Set it to yes for clients in a dispute or on a special arrangement, and filter those out.
Send message 3 to yourself first as a draft or approval email until you trust the setup.
Test with your own email address and fake invoices before pointing it at real clients.
Add an error notification so a failed run alerts you instead of failing quietly.

sections.heading: What to watch for
points: Wrong due dates in the sheet send the wrong message, so check the date format.
Late fees and interest rules vary by country and contract. Check yours before mentioning them.
Do not chase a client who has told you payment is on the way. Pause them manually.
Review the replies. The automation sends, but a person should answer.
This is education, not legal or financial advice.
